newsitem.title: FRANCE: Magistrate turns down Jewish property probe job.
newsitem.headline: Magistrate turns down Jewish property probe job.

text.p: A French Jewish magistrate has rejected a government offer to head a commission to probe the scope of property seizures by the Nazis and their Vichy French collaborators in World War Two, a deputy mayor of Paris said.

Lucien Finel, himself a Holocaust survivor, told a symposium discussing the issue late on Wednesday that the government had almost formed the five-member commission but the man chosen to head it had declined.
"He is a very respected and high-ranking magistrate and is Jewish...but he turned it down," said Finel. He declined to name the magistrate or say why he turned down the job.

He denied that he was referring to Robert Badinter, a former French justice minister but, when several people in the audience called out the name of Pierre Drai, he smiled and said: "Well, I'm not the one who said so."
Algeria-born Drai, 70, is a retired president of the Cour de Cassation, France's supreme court.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe told Jewish leaders at the weekend that the commission would be set up to tackle a dark part of the 1940-1944 Nazi occupation, a period which historians increasingly call "a past which will not pass away."

Juppe's decision followed increasing demands for the government to clarify the status of an unknown amount of property never returned to its rightful owners after the war, mostly because they were killed in gas chambers.
One recent book said authorities in 1944 took over from the retreating Germans, and still administered, possibly hundreds of flats left vacant by Jews killed in concentration camps.
A government body has determined that nearly 2,000 works of art seized from Jews were still "provisionally" in the care of French museums more than 50 years after the war.

Juppe's announcement followed moves to shed light on the dark years of World War Two in other countries including neutral Switzerland and Sweden, which both been accused of profitably dealing with the Nazis and being paid in gold seized from Jews.

"This is not a question of monetary compensation. It is a moral issue where the truth must be made known so that we can make peace with the past," said Henri Hajdenberg, president of the Council of French Jewish Institution (CRIF).
But Nazi hunters Serge and Arno Klarsfeld said the government should recommend compensation of orphans excluded from reparations paid after the war because their parents were not French nationals.

They said personal items seized from Jews on their arrest were left at Paris police headquarters and possibly 12 million francs ($2.2 million) in jewellery, watches and other personal belongings had since "disappeared" into the dark corners of the administration.
About 76,000 of the 320,000 Jews then in France were sent to Nazi concentration camps and only about 2,800 of those who were deported survived.
